youtube_title: The Jaffa Cake Trial: Cake or Biscuit? 🦝⚖️
caption: UK VAT treats chocolate-covered biscuits and cakes differently. A tribunal weighed ingredients, texture, staling, size, packaging and more, and ruled Jaffa Cakes are cakes.
script: An entire tax trial came down to one question: is this snack a cake? [disclaimer] Here's why it mattered. In Britain, most food is zero-rated for VAT. But biscuits covered in chocolate are taxed at the standard rate, while cakes, even with chocolate on them, are not. Jaffa Cakes have a sponge base, an orange layer and a chocolate top. So the tax authority decided they were really chocolate-covered biscuits, and should be taxed. The maker, United Biscuits, took it to a VAT tribunal. And the tribunal went through the evidence like a trial. The name? Only a minor point. The ingredients? An egg, flour and sugar batter, like a sponge cake. The texture? Soft sponge, not a crisp snap. And the famous one: when a Jaffa Cake goes stale, it goes hard, like a cake. A stale biscuit goes soft. Some factors pointed the other way: the size, the packaging, and the fact that shops sell them next to biscuits. But on balance, the tribunal said: cake. So Jaffa Cakes stayed zero-rated. Going hard when stale wasn't the whole test, just one factor among many. And this is one VAT result, not a rule that any snack can call itself a cake. [loop] So before you call it a biscuit, remember
